subject: Cognitive Science
title: Interference Theory
description: A short lesson to help you apply Interference Theory.

hook.text: Learn French, then learn Spanish. Suddenly your French gets worse. The new learning interfered.

buildup.text: Retroactive interference: new learning disrupts old memories. Proactive: old learning disrupts new ones.

discovery.text: The more similar two sets of material, the more they interfere. Spanish hurts French more than math does.

twist.text: Sleep between learning sessions reduces interference because consolidation locks in the first set.

climax.text: Interference isn't a bug—it reflects how memories compete for the same retrieval cues.

punchline.text: Memories don't vanish. They get outcompeted.

quiz.question: What is retroactive interference?
options: New learning disrupts recall of old material

details.summary: Interference theory explains forgetting as competition between memories. Proactive interference occurs when old memories block new learning. Retroactive interference occurs when new learning disrupts old memories. The more similar the competing materials, the stronger the interference.
details.whyItMatters: Interference is a major cause of forgetting in everyday life. Understanding it helps explain why learning similar material back-to-back causes confusion.
takeaways: Old memories can block new learning (proactive interference)
New learning can disrupt old memories (retroactive interference)

faq.question: What is a real-world example of proactive interference?
faq.answer: After moving, you keep accidentally driving to your old house. The well-established old route interferes with the new one. Similarly, learning Spanish after French is harder because French vocabulary intrudes. The older, stronger memory actively competes with the new one.

faq.question: How can you reduce interference between similar materials?
faq.answer: Space out learning of similar topics. Study French and chemistry on the same day rather than French and Spanish. Sleep between learning sessions, which consolidates memories and reduces vulnerability to interference. Distinctive encoding also helps differentiate competing memories.
